title: Amid Escalating Threats, Top Trump Officials Seek Refuge in Military Housing
snippet: With security concerns on the rise, several high-ranking members of President Donald Trump's administration are moving onto U.S. military bases, sparking debate over base resources and taxpayer costs.
content:
In an unprecedented trend driven by mounting security concerns, a growing number of top officials in President Donald Trump’s administration are moving onto U.S. military bases in the Washington, D.C., area—residences traditionally reserved for high-ranking military generals and admirals.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently revealed he relocated to a military installation following unspecified threats linked to Iran. Addressing the situation publicly, Bessent signaled that the pressure campaign would not stall his agenda. "If the Iranians are after me, it means that they are being squeezed. We’re going to continue squeezing them," Bessent remarked.

High-Profile Cabinet Members Move On Base

Bessent is far from the only administration official seeking base security. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth are currently neighbors at Fort Lesley J. McNair in the nation's capital. White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and his family also moved into military housing following what administration aides described as an intense campaign of stalking, doxing, and harassment targeting their private Virginia residence.

Other prominent figures who have utilized military housing include Attorney General Todd Blanche, former Attorney General Pam Bondi, and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, who previously stayed at Joint Base Anacostia-Bolling.

Congressional Oversight and Cost Concerns

While military installations offer robust perimeter protection and existing security infrastructure, the influx of civilian leadership has drawn sharp scrutiny on Capitol Hill. Questions have emerged regarding whether political appointees are taking housing away from senior military personnel and whether taxpayers are footing unreasonable bills.

Attention has focused on planned expenditures for these arrangements, including an estimated $137,297 in upgrades and repairs for Defense Secretary Hegseth's residence at Fort McNair. In response, lawmakers such as Rep. George Whitesides, D-Calif., have pushed for tighter oversight, requesting detailed reports from the Pentagon on the legal authorities allowing political appointees to reside on bases and confirmation that they are paying fair-market rental rates.

A Mounting Security Strategy

While civilian Cabinet officials residing on military installations was once a rare exception—first popularized under Defense Secretary Robert Gates during the Bush and Obama administrations to save on 24/7 private security costs—it has rapidly become a standard protective strategy for officials facing modern security threats.
